options.text: Split the meeting into two shorter sessions, one for the mechanical disciplines and one for the rest, each held at a different time of day.
options.rationale: It halves the attendance but keeps the readout format, and it separates the disciplines whose interfaces cause most shutdown problems. Cross-discipline issues would fall between the two meetings.

options.text: Restructure the agenda to deal with blocked work and decisions needed first, and take only exceptions from each discipline after that.
options.rationale: Putting decisions first means they are made while the right people are still in the room. Taking exceptions only keeps the meeting on what needs coordinating.

options.text: Move the meeting to the end of the shift, when the leads are no longer needed on the plant and can give the discussion their full attention.
options.rationale: It solves the timing complaint but not the format, and it pushes every decision to the end of the day. In a shutdown that can cost a whole shift on blocked work.

options.text: Ask each lead to send you a written report instead, and replace the meeting with a summary email that you send to all the leads every morning.
options.rationale: It removes the forum where cross-discipline problems get solved face to face and turns the project manager into a relay for every issue. Coordination slows rather than speeds up.

questions.explanation: A status meeting is expensive time, so it should be spent on what only a meeting can do: resolving problems that cross disciplines and taking decisions. Progress that can be read belongs in the shared artifact beforehand, handled by exception, and the agenda should put blocked work first so decisions are made while the right people are present. Changing when or how often a readout happens leaves the readout in place.
questions.mindset: Read the status, meet about the problems.

questions.stem: Your team is building an e-lending app for a regional library service. Its definition of done requires code review, automated tests and deployment to the staging environment. Reviewing the release burn-up, you find that 14 of the 52 stories counted as done in the last three sprints were merged but never deployed to staging, and several have no tests. The release is forecast as on track. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Add a 'done pending deployment' column to the board so the 14 stories stay visible without changing the velocity history the forecast relies on.
options.rationale: It makes the stories visible but keeps them counted, so the burn-up and forecast still overstate progress. It protects the comparability of the history at the expense of its truth.

options.text: Recount those 14 stories as not done, republish the burn-up and release forecast, and explain the restatement to the stakeholders who use them.
options.rationale: Stories that miss the definition of done are undone work. Restating the artifacts, and telling the people who rely on them why, puts the forecast back on the true position.

options.text: Schedule a hardening sprint before the release to deploy and test the 14 stories, keeping the current forecast and burn-up unchanged in the meantime.
options.rationale: It plans the missing work but goes on reporting it as complete until then. The hardening sprint is itself evidence that the forecast is wrong, while the chart says it is right.

options.text: Have the product owner accept stories at the sprint review only against the definition of done, with the checklist visible on the team board.
options.rationale: The inflation got in through acceptance, so that is where the rule has to be applied. A visible checklist at review keeps the count honest from now on.

options.text: Relax the definition of done for this release to merged and reviewed, and move the staging deployment and tests into a later release.
options.rationale: It changes the rule to fit what happened, so the reports become accurate by lowering the bar. The untested code and deployment work do not go away; they become unplanned debt.

questions.explanation: Progress measured against a definition of done is only as true as the definition's enforcement. Work that misses it is undone work, and counting it as done borrows from the end of the release. When inflation is found, restate the artifacts that depend on it and tell their readers, then fix the acceptance step so the count stays honest. Extra columns or hardening sprints manage the undone work but leave the forecast overstating where the release stands.
questions.mindset: Done means done against the definition, or the chart is reporting hope.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is upgrading a toll road's payment systems. A formal notice about planned lane closures went to the regulator's former liaison officer, who left five months ago, because the stakeholder register and communications plan were never updated, and the notice missed its deadline. A quick check finds other entries out of date too. The registers were written at initiation and have no named owners. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask the PMO to audit every programme artifact against current reality and report all the discrepancies it finds within the next month.
options.rationale: An audit finds drift after the fact and places responsibility with the PMO rather than with anyone who could keep the registers current. A month is also a long time to leave the known errors in place.

options.text: Correct the regulator's entry now, reissue the notice to the current liaison officer, and agree with the regulator how to handle the missed deadline.
options.rationale: The immediate harm is a regulatory notice that never arrived. Correcting the record and repairing the communication come before fixing the mechanism, because the deadline has already passed.

options.text: Require the communications lead to confirm each recipient by telephone before any formal notice is sent to a regulator or other external stakeholder.
options.rationale: It adds a control at the point of sending while the registers themselves stay stale. Every other use of those registers, from engagement planning to escalation routes, remains wrong.

options.text: Give each register a named owner and define events, such as staff changes at a stakeholder, that trigger an update between scheduled reviews.
options.rationale: The registers decayed because nobody owned them and nothing prompted a review. An owner plus event triggers addresses the cause and catches the next change when it happens.

options.text: Move all the programme's registers into a single collaborative tool so that anyone who spots an outdated entry can correct it immediately.
options.rationale: A shared tool makes editing easy but does not make it anyone's job. When everyone can update an entry, in practice no one is responsible for keeping it right.

questions.explanation: An artifact stays current only if someone owns it and something prompts them to update it; a register written at initiation with no owner and no trigger decays from the first organisational change. When decay has already caused harm, deal with the consequence first by correcting the record and repairing the communication, then fix the mechanism so the next change is caught. Audits find drift after the fact, and shared editing without ownership tends to mean nobody edits.
questions.mindset: Every living artifact needs an owner and a reason to be reopened.

questions.stem: A games studio's delivery lead receives three requests for forecasts this month. Match each situation to the forecasting approach that fits it best. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A team with twelve sprints of steady velocity must tell the publisher in which sprint a fixed set of 140 remaining story points is likely to finish.
A live-operations team works a Kanban flow of player-reported bugs of very mixed size, and the producer asks when all 40 open bugs will be cleared.
A team formed this month, with no delivery history together, is asked for an early indication of how long a new multiplayer mode will take.

options.text: Divide the remaining points by the team's lowest and highest recent velocities and quote the resulting range of sprints
options.rationale: Stable velocity on consistently sized work is good evidence, and using the low and high values turns it into an honest range rather than a single date that hides the variation.

options.text: Run a Monte Carlo simulation over the team's weekly throughput history and quote a date at a stated probability
options.rationale: Unestimated items of mixed size suit throughput sampling: the simulation uses what the team has actually finished per week and gives the producer a date with a known confidence.

options.text: Give a wide range based on comparable features built elsewhere in the studio, state the low confidence, and narrow it after a few sprints
options.rationale: With no history of its own, the team's best evidence is a reference class of similar work. Stating the low confidence and committing to narrow the range is what keeps an early figure from hardening into a promise.

options.text: Add up the developers' hour estimates for every remaining task and divide by the hours the team has available
options.rationale: Not used. Summing task-hour estimates replaces measured performance with optimism and needs a detailed task breakdown that none of the three situations has. It also produces a single figure with no sense of its uncertainty.

questions.explanation: A forecast should be built from the best evidence the team actually has: its own measured rate where there is history and the work is sized consistently, its throughput distribution where items vary and are not estimated, and comparison with similar past work where there is no history yet. Every forecast is quoted as a range or a probability, because a single number hides the uncertainty its reader most needs to see.
questions.mindset: Forecast from the evidence you have, and show how uncertain it is.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is building a new hospital wing and the software that will manage patient flow through it. Match each artifact to the way changes to it should be controlled. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The issued-for-construction drawings of the plant room, from which the mechanical contractor's crews are working on site.
The architecture decision records in which the software teams have documented the design choices they accepted over the past year.
The software teams' working agreement covering core hours, code-review turnaround and how they handle urgent production fixes.

options.text: Issue each new revision through the document register, recording it and withdrawing superseded copies from site
options.rationale: People are building from these drawings, so the danger is a crew working from an old revision. A register of current revisions and withdrawal of superseded copies is what prevents it.

options.text: Leave each accepted record unchanged and capture any reversal as a new record that states which one it supersedes
options.rationale: A decision record is valuable because it shows what was decided and why at the time. Editing it erases that history; a superseding record keeps both the old reasoning and the new.

options.text: Let the team revise it itself, usually at a retrospective, keeping the current version visible to everyone it affects
options.rationale: A working agreement belongs to the people it binds. They revise it as they learn, and keeping the current version visible is what makes it an agreement rather than a forgotten document.

options.text: Have the PMO update it each month from the workstream status returns and circulate the new version to all leads
options.rationale: Not used. Monthly central updating suits a compiled report, not any of these. It would let construction drawings lag behind site, rewrite decision history, and take a team's own agreement out of its hands.

questions.explanation: Artifacts differ in how they should change because they do different jobs. Documents that others build from need strict revision control so nobody works from a superseded copy; records of decisions keep their value by not being rewritten, so a changed decision becomes a new record pointing at the old one; and working agreements belong to the people they bind, who revise them as they learn. Choosing the control to fit the artifact's job, and its owner, keeps each one trustworthy.
questions.mindset: Control an artifact according to who relies on it and what for.

questions.stem: You are forecasting the cost at completion of three packages in a public-health laboratory fit-out for this month's report. Complete each sentence with the forecasting basis that fits the cause of each package's variance. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The electrical package overran by €80,000 because an unexpected asbestos find had to be cleared, and the remaining electrical work is unaffected, so its estimate at completion should be based on

The joinery package has run at a CPI of 0.85 for five months because the specified panels take longer to fit than the estimator allowed, and the same panels fill the rest of the package, so its estimate at completion should be based on

The ventilation package's original estimate left out the clean-room filtration system altogether, so the existing budget no longer describes the work left to do, and its estimate at completion should be based on

options.text: the actual cost to date plus the remaining work at its original budgeted cost
options.rationale: The cause was a one-off and has been dealt with, so the rest of the package should cost what was budgeted. Scaling the remaining work by the CPI would project an asbestos find onto work that has none.

options.text: the budget at completion divided by the package's cumulative cost performance index
options.rationale: The cause is built into the remaining work, so the efficiency seen so far is the best predictor of the rest. Five consistent months and an unchanged specification support assuming it continues.

options.text: the actual cost to date plus a fresh bottom-up estimate of the remaining work
options.rationale: When the original estimate missed work entirely, no index applied to it can recover the missing scope. The remaining work has to be estimated again from what is now known.

options.text: the actual cost to date plus the remaining work divided by the product of the cost and schedule indices
options.rationale: Not used. Combining both indices fits a case where a fixed completion date is forcing acceleration, so schedule performance drives future cost too. None of the three packages describes that pressure.

questions.explanation: The forecasting formula is a statement about the future: whether the cause of the variance has stopped, will continue, or has shown the original estimate to be wrong. Identifying the cause comes first and the formula follows from it. A one-off cause leaves the remaining budget valid, a persistent one scales it by performance to date, and a broken estimate needs replacing rather than adjusting. Combined cost and schedule indices belong where a fixed date is making schedule pressure drive cost.
questions.mindset: Find out why a variance happened before deciding what it says about the rest.

questions.stem: A ten-month motorway resurfacing contract has cumulative planned value, in £000, of 60, 150, 260, 380, 500, 610, 700, 780, 850 and 900 at the end of months 1 to 10. At the end of month 7, earned value is £555,000. The client wants the delay stated in months rather than pounds. Earned schedule is the time at which planned value equalled today's earned value, interpolating linearly within a month.

blanks.label: Earned schedule, in months, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: Earned value of 555 falls between planned value of 500 at month 5 and 610 at month 6. Interpolating: 5 + (555 − 500) ÷ (610 − 500) = 5 + 55 ÷ 110 = 5.5 months. The work done by month 7 was planned to be done by mid-month 6.

blanks.label: Time-based schedule performance index (earned schedule ÷ actual time), to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: Actual time is 7 months, so the index is 5.5 ÷ 7 = 0.786, about 0.79. The project is achieving roughly 79% of a month's planned progress for each month that passes, which puts it 1.5 months behind.

blanks.label: Forecast total duration if this time performance continues (planned duration ÷ time-based index), in months, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: Planned duration of 10 months divided by 0.786 gives 12.7 months, a finish about 2.7 months late if the current rate continues. The cost-based schedule variance of −£145,000 says nothing directly about this date.

questions.explanation: Earned value variances are measured in money, and as a late project approaches its end the cost-based schedule variance shrinks towards zero because all the planned value is eventually earned, however late the finish. Translating earned value onto the time axis, by finding when the plan expected today's achievement, gives a schedule measure that stays meaningful to the end and answers the question clients actually ask. Report slippage in units of time whenever the audience is planning around dates.
questions.mindset: Answer a question about dates in units of time.

questions.stem: The tracking Gantt for a hospice extension shows five activities. Each label gives how far the activity's forecast finish has slipped against baseline and the total float it had in the baseline schedule. The trustees ask which delay, if any, you should report as threatening the contractual handover date. Select that activity.

graphic.title: Tracking Gantt: five activities with slippage against baseline and baseline total float
graphic.caption: Select an activity. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Ward fit-out: 12 days behind baseline, 20 days total float
regions.rationale: A twelve-day slip looks serious, but the activity had twenty days of float and still has eight. Choosing it ranks delays by size rather than by what they do to the finish date.

regions.label: Nurse-call installation: 6 days behind baseline, 6 days total float
regions.rationale: The slip has used exactly all of the float, so the activity is now critical and should be watched closely. But it has not yet moved the handover date, and reporting it as the threat confuses zero float with negative float.

regions.label: Medical gas testing: 5 days behind baseline, 2 days total float
regions.rationale: The slip exceeds the float by three days, so unless it is recovered the handover moves by three days. It is one of the smaller delays on the chart and the only one that reaches the finish.

regions.label: Garden landscaping: 15 days behind baseline, 30 days total float
regions.rationale: The largest slip on the chart, which is what draws the eye, but it has used only half its float. Picking it treats calendar delay as if it were schedule risk.

regions.label: Lift commissioning: on baseline, 0 days total float
regions.rationale: This activity is on the critical path, so any slip would move handover, but it has not slipped. Being critical is a reason to watch an activity, not evidence that it is threatening the date.

questions.explanation: A delay threatens the end date only when it exceeds the float the activity had, so reading a tracking Gantt means comparing each slip with its float rather than ranking slips by size. The largest delay is often harmless, an activity whose float is exactly used up has become critical and needs watching, and a modest slip on a low-float activity can be the one that moves the finish. Report the threat as the number of days by which slip exceeds float.
questions.mindset: Judge a delay by the float it consumes, not by its size.
